claim: Manipulative experiments and observations along environmental gradients are the two most common approaches to evaluate the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling.
source: Manipulative experiments and observations along environmental gradients, the two most common approaches to evaluate the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling, are generally assumed to produce similar results, but this assumption has rarely been tested.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Manipulative experiments and observations along environmental gradients are generally assumed to produce similar results.
source: Manipulative experiments and observations along environmental gradients, the two most common approaches to evaluate the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling, are generally assumed to produce similar results, but this assumption has rarely been tested.
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in the field.

claim: The assumption that manipulative experiments and observations along environmental gradients produce similar results has rarely been tested.
source: Manipulative experiments and observations along environmental gradients, the two most common approaches to evaluate the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling, are generally assumed to produce similar results, but this assumption has rarely been tested.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Soil carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus concentrations generally decreased with water addition in manipulative experiments.
source: Soil carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus concentrations generally decreased with water addition in manipulative experiments but increased with annual precipitation along environmental gradients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis of experimental studies.

claim: Soil carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus concentrations increased with annual precipitation along environmental gradients.
source: Soil carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus concentrations generally decreased with water addition in manipulative experiments but increased with annual precipitation along environmental gradients.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis of observational studies.

claim: Different patterns were observed between warming experiments and temperature gradients.
source: Different patterns were also observed between warming experiments and temperature gradients.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Manipulative experiments may be better predictors of the causal impacts of short-term (months to years) climate change on soil nutrients.
source: Our findings provide evidence of inconsistent results and suggest that manipulative experiments may be better predictors of the causal impacts of short-term (months to years) climate change on soil nutrients but environmental gradients may provide better information for long-term correlations (centuries to millennia) between these nutrients and climatic features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Environmental gradients may provide better information for long-term correlations (centuries to millennia) between soil nutrients and climatic features.
source: Our findings provide evidence of inconsistent results and suggest that manipulative experiments may be better predictors of the causal impacts of short-term (months to years) climate change on soil nutrients but environmental gradients may provide better information for long-term correlations (centuries to millennia) between these nutrients and climatic features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Ecosystem models should incorporate both experimental and observational data to properly assess the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling.
source: Ecosystem models should consequently incorporate both experimental and observational data to properly assess the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Shifts in patterns of precipitation and increases in temperature are two major components of ongoing climate change.
source: Shifts in patterns of precipitation and increases in temperature are two major components of ongoing climate change (IPCC, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the IPCC 2014 report.

claim: Manipulative experiments and observational studies constitute the main empirical approaches typically used to forecast ecological responses to climate change.
source: Manipulative experiments (e.g. field/mesocosm) and observational studies constitute the main empirical approaches typically used to forecast ecological responses to climate change (Beier et al., 2012; Kreyling and Beier, 2013; Michelsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The major difference between manipulative experiments and observational studies is likely the issue of association versus causation.
source: The major difference between these approaches is likely the issue of association versus causation; observational studies randomly select a sample of subjects and may find correlations between variables (Rosenbaum, 2010; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: Observational studies randomly select a sample of subjects and may find correlations between variables.
source: The major difference between these approaches is likely the issue of association versus causation; observational studies randomly select a sample of subjects and may find correlations between variables (Rosenbaum, 2010; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: Experimental studies can identify and confirm the potential mechanisms underlying observed responses by controlling any variable.
source: In comparison, experimental studies can identify and confirm the potential mechanisms underlying observed responses by controlling any variable (Montgomery, 2008) and can assess cause-effect relationships based on the direct effects of climate change on small-scale, rapid, and short-term ecological processes (Chapin and Shaver, 1996; Tilman, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: Experimental studies can assess cause-effect relationships based on the direct effects of climate change on small-scale, rapid, and short-term ecological processes.
source: In comparison, experimental studies can identify and confirm the potential mechanisms underlying observed responses by controlling any variable (Montgomery, 2008) and can assess cause-effect relationships based on the direct effects of climate change on small-scale, rapid, and short-term ecological processes (Chapin and Shaver, 1996; Tilman, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: If an experimental study is well-controlled, the factor that causes the difference can be reliably identified.
source: If an experimental study is well-controlled, the factor that causes the difference can be reliably identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of controlled experiments.

claim: All confounding factors cannot be ruled out in observational studies.
source: In contrast, all confounding factors cannot be ruled out in observational studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of observational studies.

claim: Experimental responses are generally assumed to mimic long-term responses to climate change.
source: Experimental responses are generally assumed to mimic long-term responses to climate change (Luo and Hui, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Biomass production shows similar positive responses to both experimental and spatial gradients of increasing temperature and water availability.
source: This assumption may be due to the similar positive responses of biomass production to both experimental and spatial gradients of increasing temperature and water availability (Lin et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2013; Rustad et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Recent studies challenge the assumption that experimental responses mimic long-term responses to climate change.
source: Recent studies, however, challenge this critical but largely unexplored assumption (Blume-Werry et al., 2016; Metz and Tielboerger, 2016; Primack et al., 2015; Wolkovich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: The direction and magnitude of observed impacts of climate change on ecosystems largely depend on whether the data are observational or experimental.
source: Indeed, the direction and magnitude of observed impacts of climate change on ecosystems largely depend on whether the data are observational or experimental (Metz and Tielboerger, 2016; Osmond et al., 2004; Sternberg et al., 2011; Wolkovich et al., 2012), and these discrepancies have led to debates on the relevance of results of manipulative experiments for natural communities (Hewitt et al., 2007; Sagarin and Pauchard, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Discrepancies between observational and experimental approaches have led to debates on the relevance of results of manipulative experiments for natural communities.
source: Indeed, the direction and magnitude of observed impacts of climate change on ecosystems largely depend on whether the data are observational or experimental (Metz and Tielboerger, 2016; Osmond et al., 2004; Sternberg et al., 2011; Wolkovich et al., 2012), and these discrepancies have led to debates on the relevance of results of manipulative experiments for natural communities (Hewitt et al., 2007; Sagarin and Pauchard, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Soils are intricately linked to the atmospheric climate system through biogeochemical and hydrological cycles.
source: Soils are intricately linked to the atmospheric climate system through biogeochemical and hydrological cycles (Chapin et al., 2011; Jarvie et al., 2012; Williams, 1987), hence any change in climate is expected to influence soil characteristics and vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Any change in climate is expected to influence soil characteristics and vice versa.
source: Soils are intricately linked to the atmospheric climate system through biogeochemical and hydrological cycles (Chapin et al., 2011; Jarvie et al., 2012; Williams, 1987), hence any change in climate is expected to influence soil characteristics and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linkage between soils and climate.

claim: Climate change will impact soil processes and properties, with critical consequences for the biogeochemical cycles of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus.
source: Research in the last two decades has suggested various ways in which climate change will impact soil processes and properties, with critical consequences for the biogeochemical cycles of carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) (Field et al., 2007; Hungate et al., 2003; Thornton et al., 2009; van Groenigen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The direction and magnitude of climate change impacts on soil nutrients largely depend on changes in precipitation and temperature.
source: The direction and magnitude of these impacts largely depend on changes in precipitation and temperature, which are key drivers of biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about climate impacts on soil nutrients.

claim: Precipitation and temperature are key drivers of biogeochemical cycles.
source: The direction and magnitude of these impacts largely depend on changes in precipitation and temperature, which are key drivers of biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Results from studies on climate impacts on soil nutrients may vary greatly depending on whether the data are from observational or experimental studies.
source: The results from these studies, however, may vary greatly depending on whether the data are from observational or experimental studies (Metz and Tielboerger, 2016; Osmond et al., 2004; Sternberg et al., 2011; Wolkovich et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Spatial data across natural gradients of precipitation or temperature are abundant.
source: Little information from long-term historical observations of soil nutrients is available, but spatial data across natural gradients of precipitation or temperature are abundant, offering an invaluable source for understanding the impacts of climate change on natural ecosystems at long-term scales.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about data availability.

claim: Little information from long-term historical observations of soil nutrients is available.
source: Little information from long-term historical observations of soil nutrients is available, but spatial data across natural gradients of precipitation or temperature are abundant, offering an invaluable source for understanding the impacts of climate change on natural ecosystems at long-term scales.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about data availability.

claim: Climate change largely influences key ecosystem processes, including those involving soil nutrients.
source: Results from both experiments and natural observations indicate that climate change largely influences key ecosystem processes, including those involving soil nutrients (Elmendorf et al., 2015; Sternberg and Yakir, 2015; Wolkovich et al., 2012; Yuan and Chen, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Much less is known about the agreement between experimental and observational approaches for the direction and magnitude of the responses of nutrient cycling to climate change.
source: Much less is known, however, about the agreement between experimental and observational approaches for the direction and magnitude of the responses of nutrient cycling to climate change.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Differences in approaches are often theoretically recognized but have rarely been empirically evaluated and quantified.
source: In effect, differences in approaches are often theoretically recognized (De Boeck et al., 2015; Dunne et al., 2004; Jiang et al., 2009) but have rarely been empirically evaluated and quantified.
evidence: This is supported by citations and stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Experiments that directly manipulate species diversity often report a positive effect of diversity on productivity.
source: Biodiversity–productivity relationships contain an apparent paradox: experiments that directly manipulate species diversity often report a positive effect of diversity on productivity, whereas observations of natural communities identify various productivity–diversity relationships (Jiang et al., 2009; Wardle and Jonsson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Observations of natural communities identify various productivity–diversity relationships.
source: Biodiversity–productivity relationships contain an apparent paradox: experiments that directly manipulate species diversity often report a positive effect of diversity on productivity, whereas observations of natural communities identify various productivity–diversity relationships (Jiang et al., 2009; Wardle and Jonsson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Short-term experiments of N fertilization reported nearly ubiquitous negative productivity–diversity relationships.
source: Short-term experiments of N fertilization reported nearly ubiquitous negative productivity–diversity relationships (Suding et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Experiments usually detect negative diversity–invasibility relationships.
source: Contrasting patterns may be found for the diversity–invasibility relationship: experiments usually detect negative relationships, and field surveys find positive relationships (Clark et al., 2013; Fridley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Field surveys find positive diversity–invasibility relationships.
source: Contrasting patterns may be found for the diversity–invasibility relationship: experiments usually detect negative relationships, and field surveys find positive relationships (Clark et al., 2013; Fridley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: A wealth of data for soil nutrients is available for testing the consistency between experimental and observational approaches.
source: Fortunately, compared with the lack of data for other ecosystem response variables (e.g. species diversity, gas exchange, and microbial attributes), a wealth of data for soil nutrients is available for testing the consistency between experimental and observational approaches.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about data availability.

claim: The meta-analysis included 1421 data points from 182 experimental studies.
source: We thus conducted a meta-analysis of 1421 data points from 182 experimental studies and of a total of 1346 sites from 141 studies of natural gradients around the world (see Figure 1 and Supplementary References).
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: The meta-analysis included a total of 1346 sites from 141 studies of natural gradients around the world.
source: We thus conducted a meta-analysis of 1421 data points from 182 experimental studies and of a total of 1346 sites from 141 studies of natural gradients around the world (see Figure 1 and Supplementary References).
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: Total nutrient concentrations represent long-term nutrient reservoirs in terrestrial ecosystems.
source: We used total nutrient concentrations because they represent long-term nutrient reservoirs in terrestrial ecosystems and are more stable than extractable nutrients in soils.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the choice of measurement.

claim: Total nutrient concentrations are more stable than extractable nutrients in soils.
source: We used total nutrient concentrations because they represent long-term nutrient reservoirs in terrestrial ecosystems and are more stable than extractable nutrients in soils.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the choice of measurement.

claim: Total C, N, and P concentrations generally indicate overall nutrient availability.
source: Total C, N, and P concentrations generally indicate overall nutrient availability and are positively correlated with each other (Bertiller et al., 2006; Jacoby, 2005; Silver, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Total C, N, and P concentrations are positively correlated with each other.
source: Total C, N, and P concentrations generally indicate overall nutrient availability and are positively correlated with each other (Bertiller et al., 2006; Jacoby, 2005; Silver, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Temperature varies across precipitation gradients.
source: Given that temperature varies across precipitation gradients we also used aridity, which incorporates both potential evapotranspiration and precipitation.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using aridity as a variable.

claim: Aridity incorporates both potential evapotranspiration and precipitation.
source: Given that temperature varies across precipitation gradients we also used aridity, which incorporates both potential evapotranspiration and precipitation.
evidence: This is stated as a definition of aridity.

claim: Short-term local manipulative experiments and large-scale observational studies identify different responses of soil nutrients to changes in climatic conditions.
source: We hypothesized that short-term local manipulative experiments and large-scale observational studies identify different responses of soil nutrients to changes in climatic conditions.
evidence: This is stated as the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: The properties of ecosystems often respond in a simultaneous and predictive manner to slow changes in climate.
source: The properties of ecosystems thus often respond in a simultaneous and predictive manner to slow changes in climate (e.g. plant cover, diversity, soil properties and nutrient pools), but rapid climatic changes will likely disrupt the simultaneous responses of these slowly changing processes to climate change.
evidence: This is stated as part of the hypothesis rationale.

claim: Rapid climatic changes will likely disrupt the simultaneous responses of slowly changing ecosystem processes to climate change.
source: The properties of ecosystems thus often respond in a simultaneous and predictive manner to slow changes in climate (e.g. plant cover, diversity, soil properties and nutrient pools), but rapid climatic changes will likely disrupt the simultaneous responses of these slowly changing processes to climate change.
evidence: This is stated as part of the hypothesis rationale.

claim: A change in water supply in manipulative precipitation experiments could directly influence the balance between nutrient uptake/leaching vs. mineralization/decomposition, particularly in arid ecosystems.
source: For example, a change in water supply in manipulative precipitation experiments in local environments (e.g. similar plant species, plant cover, or soil type) could directly influence the balance between nutrient uptake/leaching vs. mineralization/decomposition, particularly in arid ecosystems (Ansley et al., 2014; Davidson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in the diversity and cover of vascular plants.
source: For example, increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in the diversity and cover of vascular plants, rates of litter decomposition, and availability of C and N (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2013; Jiao et al., 2016), all of which co-evolve over millennia (Ehrenfeld et al., 2005; Lambers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in rates of litter decomposition.
source: For example, increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in the diversity and cover of vascular plants, rates of litter decomposition, and availability of C and N (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2013; Jiao et al., 2016), all of which co-evolve over millennia (Ehrenfeld et al., 2005; Lambers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in availability of C and N.
source: For example, increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in the diversity and cover of vascular plants, rates of litter decomposition, and availability of C and N (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2013; Jiao et al., 2016), all of which co-evolve over millennia (Ehrenfeld et al., 2005; Lambers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Plant diversity, cover, litter decomposition rates, and C and N availability co-evolve over millennia.
source: For example, increases in aridity across a gradient often lead to reductions in the diversity and cover of vascular plants, rates of litter decomposition, and availability of C and N (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2013; Jiao et al., 2016), all of which co-evolve over millennia (Ehrenfeld et al., 2005; Lambers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Short-term local manipulative experiments could provide useful information for predicting shifts in soil processes in response to rapid changes in climate (from years to decades).
source: We thus posit that short-term local manipulative experiments could provide useful information for predicting shifts in soil processes in response to rapid changes in climate (from years to decades, e.g. drought), such as those we are facing today.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: Observational studies might provide unique information for understanding the response of soil processes to long-term changes in climate (from centuries to thousands of years).
source: In contrast, observational studies might provide unique information for understanding the response of soil processes to long-term changes in climate (from centuries to thousands of years, e.g. increases in aridity [Huang et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis, with a citation to support the example of aridity increases.

claim: Manipulative experiments have typically been performed at short temporal scales in relatively homogeneous environments to maximize experimental control.
source: As stated above, the contrasting findings between manipulative experiments and observational studies may be due to the timescale, because the former have typically been performed at short temporal scales in relatively homogeneous environments to maximize experimental control, whereas the latter have usually been established over largely spatial gradients that reflect long-term adjustments of ecosystems to local climate (Kueppers and Harte, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Observational studies have usually been established over largely spatial gradients that reflect long-term adjustments of ecosystems to local climate.
source: As stated above, the contrasting findings between manipulative experiments and observational studies may be due to the timescale, because the former have typically been performed at short temporal scales in relatively homogeneous environments to maximize experimental control, whereas the latter have usually been established over largely spatial gradients that reflect long-term adjustments of ecosystems to local climate (Kueppers and Harte, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: The availabilities of soil nutrients reflect both short- and long-term changes in climate, soil and ecosystem development.
source: Given that the availabilities of soil nutrients reflect both short- and long-term changes in climate, soil and ecosystem development (Vitousek et al., 2010), we hypothesized, therefore, that experimental and observational studies would not produce similar results for soil nutrients in response to climate change.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Experimental and observational studies would not produce similar results for soil nutrients in response to climate change.
source: Given that the availabilities of soil nutrients reflect both short- and long-term changes in climate, soil and ecosystem development (Vitousek et al., 2010), we hypothesized, therefore, that experimental and observational studies would not produce similar results for soil nutrients in response to climate change.
evidence: This is stated as the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: Adding water in experiments decreased soil N concentration by 5.4%.
source: Overall, adding water in experiments decreased soil N, P, and C concentrations by 5.4, 9.3, and 2.7%, respectively (non-significantly for C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis.

claim: Adding water in experiments decreased soil P concentration by 9.3%.
source: Overall, adding water in experiments decreased soil N, P, and C concentrations by 5.4, 9.3, and 2.7%, respectively (non-significantly for C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis.

claim: Adding water in experiments decreased soil C concentration by 2.7% (non-significantly).
source: Overall, adding water in experiments decreased soil N, P, and C concentrations by 5.4, 9.3, and 2.7%, respectively (non-significantly for C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis.

claim: N concentration increased with precipitation across environmental gradients.
source: In contrast, N concentration increased with precipitation across environmental gradients.
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis of observational studies.

claim: The enhanced effects of increasing precipitation on C and P concentrations were not significant in observational studies.
source: The enhanced effects of increasing precipitation on C and P concentrations were not significant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Experimental drought treatments significantly increased the concentrations of C by 6.1%.
source: Experimental drought treatments significantly increased the concentrations of C, N, and P by 6.1, 17.9, and 6.8%, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis.

claim: Experimental drought treatments significantly increased the concentrations of N by 17.9%.
source: Experimental drought treatments significantly increased the concentrations of C, N, and P by 6.1, 17.9, and 6.8%, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis.

claim: Experimental drought treatments significantly increased the concentrations of P by 6.8%.
source: Experimental drought treatments significantly increased the concentrations of C, N, and P by 6.1, 17.9, and 6.8%, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the meta-analysis.

claim: Soil N concentration decreased with increasing aridity in observational studies.
source: Soil N and P concentrations decreased with increasing aridity and C concentration did not change significantly when precipitation was replaced by aridity.
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis of observational studies.

claim: Soil P concentration decreased with increasing aridity in observational studies.
source: Soil N and P concentrations decreased with increasing aridity and C concentration did not change significantly when precipitation was replaced by aridity.
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis of observational studies.

claim: Soil C concentration did not change significantly with aridity in observational studies.
source: Soil N and P concentrations decreased with increasing aridity and C concentration did not change significantly when precipitation was replaced by aridity.
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis of observational studies.

claim: The aridity-related patterns were opposite to those observed in manipulative drought experiments.
source: The aridity-related patterns were opposite to those observed in manipulative drought experiments (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of results between observational and experimental studies, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Experimental warming generally increased the concentrations of C, N, and P, especially that of N.
source: Experimental warming generally increased the concentrations of C, N, and P, especially that of N (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis of experimental studies, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Soil C, N, and P concentrations tended to decrease along gradients of increasing mean annual temperature.
source: In contrast, these concentrations tended to decrease along gradients of increasing mean annual temperature (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis of observational studies, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Patterns were inconsistent between manipulative experiments and environmental gradient observations for the same climate-change factor of precipitation or temperature across different types of ecosystems or soils.
source: Similar results were found for temperature-related changes in C, N, and P concentrations across different types of ecosystems or soils: patterns were inconsistent between manipulative experiments and environmental gradient observations for the same climate-change factor of precipitation or temperature (Figures 2–4).
evidence: This is a summary of results across different ecosystem and soil types, with reference to Figures 2-4.

claim: The response ratio of soil C concentration increased quadratically with mean annual precipitation in water-addition experiments.
source: The response ratio of soil C concentration increased quadratically with mean annual precipitation in water-addition experiments, but decreased non-significantly with precipitation in drought experiments (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The response ratio of soil C concentration decreased non-significantly with precipitation in drought experiments.
source: The response ratio of soil C concentration increased quadratically with mean annual precipitation in water-addition experiments, but decreased non-significantly with precipitation in drought experiments (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The response ratios of N and P concentrations in manipulative precipitation experiments were not significantly correlated with mean annual precipitation.
source: The response ratios of N and P concentrations in manipulative precipitation experiments were not significantly correlated with mean annual precipitation.
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis.

claim: The response ratio of P concentration in drought experiments decreased with precipitation.
source: The response ratio of P concentration in drought experiments decreased with precipitation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The relationship between response ratio of P concentration in drought experiments and precipitation was mainly dependent on two data points.
source: This relationship, however, was mainly dependent on two data points (Figure 5) and disappeared when they were removed (R2 = 0.01, p=0.84).
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The response ratio of C concentration in warming experiments was linearly correlated with mean annual temperature.
source: The response ratio of C concentration in warming experiments was linearly correlated with mean annual temperature.
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis.

claim: Unimodal curves best described the relationships between the response ratio of N and P concentrations in warming experiments and mean annual temperature.
source: Unimodal curves best described the relationships between the response ratio of N and P concentrations in warming experiments and mean annual temperature.
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis.

claim: At low to moderate levels, mean annual temperature increased the response ratio of P concentrations in warming experiments.
source: At low to moderate levels, mean annual temperature increased the response ratio of P concentrations.
evidence: This is a result from cross-study analysis.

claim: Climatic data (temperature and precipitation) collectively explained ~30% of the variation in soil total C, N, and P concentrations in observational studies.
source: In the cross-study analyses of all observational studies, climatic data (temperature and precipitation) collectively explained ~30% of the variation in soil total C, N, and P concentrations.
evidence: This is a result from multiple regression analysis.

claim: Soil and ecosystem types were also strong drivers of total C, N, and P concentrations.
source: Soil and ecosystem types were also strong drivers of total C, N, and P concentrations.
evidence: This is a result from multiple regression analysis.

claim: The variables of climate, aridity, and type of ecosystem and soil accounted for ~63–77% of the variation observed in the C, N, and P concentrations.
source: When all data were included, the variables of climate, aridity, and type of ecosystem and soil accounted for ~63–77% of the variation observed in the C, N, and P concentrations (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from multiple regression analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Soil C, N and P concentrations changed quadratically with mean annual precipitation and temperature based on all observations from the observational studies.
source: Soil C, N and P concentrations, based on all observations from the observational studies, changed quadratically with mean annual precipitation and temperature (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Both C and N concentration were significantly and positively correlated with mean annual precipitation in observational studies.
source: Both C and N concentration were significantly and positively correlated with mean annual precipitation but negatively correlated to aridity.
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of observational studies.

claim: Both C and N concentration were negatively correlated to aridity in observational studies.
source: Both C and N concentration were significantly and positively correlated with mean annual precipitation but negatively correlated to aridity.
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of observational studies.

claim: Soil P was negatively correlated with precipitation in observational studies.
source: Soil P was negatively correlated with precipitation but was not significantly correlated with the aridity.
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of observational studies.

claim: Soil P was not significantly correlated with aridity in observational studies.
source: Soil P was negatively correlated with precipitation but was not significantly correlated with the aridity.
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of observational studies.

claim: Soil C, N and P were quadratically correlated with temperature in observational studies.
source: Soil C, N and P were quadratically correlated to with temperature.
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of observational studies.

claim: Soil P concentrations increased at low level of precipitation but decreased at high level of precipitation in control plots from experiments.
source: Soil P concentrations increased at low level of precipitation but decreased at high level of precipitation.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of control plots from experiments.

claim: Neither C nor N were significantly correlated with precipitation in control plots from experiments.
source: Neither C nor N were significantly correlated with precipitation.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of control plots from experiments.

claim: Soil C, especially N and P, significantly decreased with aridity in control plots from experiments.
source: In contrast, soil C, especially N and P, significantly decreased with aridity.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of control plots from experiments.

claim: Soil C and N were negatively correlated with temperature in control plots from experiments.
source: Soil C and N were negatively correlated with temperature but soil P was positively correlated with temperature.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of control plots from experiments.

claim: Soil P was positively correlated with temperature in control plots from experiments.
source: Soil C and N were negatively correlated with temperature but soil P was positively correlated with temperature.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of control plots from experiments.

claim: Differences between observational and experimental studies evaluating biodiversity–productivity relationships could be understandable because the artificial selection of component species in short-term manipulative experiments can lead to a 'sampling' or 'positive selection' effect.
source: Differences between observational and experimental studies evaluating biodiversity–productivity relationships could be understandable because the artificial selection of component species in short-term manipulative experiments can lead to a 'sampling' or 'positive selection' effect, whereby randomly selecting a more productive species is more likely in more diverse treatments (Tilman et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Climate change tends to have a direct and simple effect on soil nutrients in the relatively homogenous environments that characterize small-scale manipulative experiments conducted at a single field site.
